title: Humour and irony
goals: Recognise and produce understatement and litotes, and infer the implied meaning.
Distinguish irony, sarcasm and other forms of humour, and detect their signals.
Use "as if" / "as though" with unreal and real situations.
Understand puns, double meanings and rhetorical devices.
React naturally to humour and to implicit meaning in English.

learn.title: Understatement and litotes: saying less to mean more
learn.html:
Understatement consists of expressing something with less intensity than the reality warrants; the listener must infer the true magnitude. It is the most characteristic feature of British humour and politeness. Litotes is a variant: denying the opposite (not bad = quite good; not unkind = rather kind).

What is saidWhat is meant (implicit)
It was a bit of an inconvenience. (after getting lost in the mountains for two days)It was a terrible experience.
Not bad at all. / It wasn't half bad.It is very good (genuine praise, but restrained).
That's an interesting idea.I'm not convinced; we'll probably not do it.
It could have gone better.It was a disaster.
I wouldn't say no to…I would love to (enthusiastic but discreet acceptance).
That's not exactly what I'd call a success.It was a failure.

Softening intensifiers. Quite, rather, fairly, a bit, slightly: in British English quite good usually means "acceptable, somewhat below expectations"; in American English it can be intensifying. Rather + positive adjective is stronger (rather good = quite good, surprisingly good).

Frequent structures: a bit of a + noun (a bit of a problem), not the best / not exactly + noun, I've had better days, Well, that could have gone better. The pragmatic key: the competent listener recognises the mismatch between the mild word and the seriousness of the situation.

watch.wrong: The food was quite good (para alabar mucho).
watch.right: The food was really good / excellent.
watch.why: In British English quite good usually means "acceptable"; if you want to praise sincerely, use really or excellent.

watch.wrong: I'm afraid there's a bit problem with your order.
watch.right: I'm afraid there's a bit of a problem with your order.
watch.why: The formula is a bit of a + noun; courteous understatement requires the full structure.

watch.wrong: Thank you a lot for ruining my day.
watch.right: Thanks a lot for ruining my day.
watch.why: Sarcastic thanks uses the fixed formula Thanks a lot; thank you a lot sounds unnatural and does not convey the irony.

watch.wrong: They made a joke of me at the party.
watch.right: They made fun of me at the party.
watch.why: Make fun of = to mock; make a joke of something means treating something lightly, not mocking a person.

learn.title: Implicature, irony and sarcasm
learn.html:
Implicature (H. P. Grice) is the meaning a speaker communicates without saying it literally. Conversation is governed by a cooperative principle: the speaker is expected to be informative, truthful, relevant and clear. When a sentence seems to break those expectations, the listener assumes there is a hidden meaning and looks for it.

UtteranceLiteral meaningImplied meaning
"Can you pass the salt?"Are you able to pass it?Please pass me the salt.
"It's a bit cold in here."It is somewhat cold.Could you close the window?
"Some of the students passed."At least one passed.Not all of them passed (scalar implicature).
"I have an exam at 8 tomorrow." (answering "Are you coming out?")I have an exam.I'm not going / I can't stay out.
"Lovely weather!" (in the rain)The weather is nice.The weather is awful (irony).

Irony: saying the opposite of what is meant (verbal), an outcome opposite to what was expected (situational irony: a fire station that burns down), or the audience knowing something the character does not (dramatic irony). Sarcasm: verbal irony with a target and a hurtful intent (Thanks, that's really helpful, said to someone who has just spilled coffee on your keyboard).

Signals for detecting them: exaggerated or deliberately flat intonation, a pause, hyperbole, an obvious mismatch with the situation, or fixed responses such as Oh, great, Brilliant, Tell me about it, That's one way of putting it (= I would put it differently, less kindly or less accurately).

watch.wrong: He told me sarcastic that I was very clever.
watch.right: He told me sarcastically that I was very clever.
watch.why: An adverb (sarcastically) is needed to modify the verb; the implication is that I was considered the opposite of clever.

watch.right: With a dry tone, 'Thanks a lot!' is usually sarcastic.
watch.why: You must attend to context and tone: what is said and what is meant can be opposites.

watch.wrong: He is a very sensible person; he cried at the joke about his dog.
watch.right: He is a very sensitive person; he cried at the joke about his dog.

watch.wrong: Interesting idea! = ¡Qué idea tan fascinante, la adoptaremos!
watch.right: 'That's an interesting idea' suele implicar reservas.
watch.why: Between British speakers it is a polite way of not committing; the implied meaning is disagreement.

learn.title: as if / as though + unreal situation
learn.html:
As if and as though compare a situation with a hypothetical manner. If the comparison is unreal or contrary to fact, the past is used (for the present) or the past perfect (for the past), even with were for all persons in formal register.

MeaningStructureExample
Unreal, presentas if + past simple (were/was)He talks as if he owned the place. (it isn't his)
Unreal, pastas if + past perfectShe reacted as if I had insulted her. (I didn't insult her)
Possible/realas if + presentIt looks as if it is going to rain. (it is possible)
Ironic reproachIt's not as if + clauseIt's not as if I cared what he thinks.
Sarcastic rejectionAs if!—He says he'll finish by tomorrow. —As if! (= I don't believe that at all)

Key nuance: the mood (indicative versus unreal past) reveals what the speaker believes. He looks as if he is ill (I think he really is) versus He behaves as if he were ill (he isn't, but he is pretending). With as though the usage is identical. In informal register, like replaces as if (He talks like he owns the place), but it is avoided in formal writing.

watch.wrong: He behaves as if he is the boss (y no lo es).
watch.right: He behaves as if he were the boss.
watch.why: Unreal situation: past (were/was), not present; the present would imply that it is the case.

watch.wrong: She looked at me as if I have two heads.
watch.right: She looked at me as if I had two heads.
watch.why: A comparison contrary to fact: past simple.

watch.wrong: It looks as if it would rain any minute.
watch.right: It looks as if it is going to rain any minute. / …as if it will rain…
watch.why: When the possibility is real, the indicative (present or future) is used, not the conditional.

watch.wrong: He spends as if he would be rich.
watch.right: He spends as if he were rich.
watch.why: "Would" is not used after "as if"; an unreal comparison requires the past simple.

learn.title: Puns, types of humour and rhetorical devices
learn.html:
Much of English humour is linguistic: it depends on a word or structure admitting two readings. Getting the joke requires activating both.

DeviceWhat it isExample and implied meaning
Pun (word play)Two similar meanings or soundsI used to be a banker, but I lost interest. Interest = banking interest / curiosity.
ZeugmaOne verb with two complements of different meaningShe lost her keys and her temper.
Double entendreA phrase with a second, often suggestive, meaningIt is said with an innocent appearance to suggest something else.
OxymoronContradictory termsdeafening silence, bitter-sweet
HyperboleDeliberate exaggerationI've told you a million times.
DeadpanHumour delivered with a straight face, without signalling the jokeThe audience must realise on their own.
Satire / parodyRidicule for a critical purpose / a mocking imitationA sketch that exaggerates a politician's habits.

Comprehension strategy: if a sentence seems absurd, illogical or unnecessarily precise in its context, there is probably a second reading. Ask yourself: which word can mean something else? What did the listener expect to be said? Who is the target of the mockery?

Humour rarely translates literally: you almost always have to reproduce the effect, not the words.

watch.wrong: He made a witty quip that everyone laughed it.
watch.right: He made a witty quip that everyone laughed at.
watch.why: Laugh at requires a preposition; the relative pronoun is omitted or placed at the beginning.

watch.wrong: The comedian made fun with the politicians.
watch.right: The comedian made fun of the politicians.
watch.why: Make fun of: to mock; with it, a target is criticised.

watch.wrong: I didn't understand the joke because was a pun.
watch.right: I didn't get the joke because it was a pun.
watch.why: The subject "it" is obligatory in English; the implication: the joke depends on two meanings.
An before a vowel sound: an ironic, an unexpected.

learn.title: Responding to implicit meaning, irony and humour
learn.html:
Marking or detecting irony: Oh, great. / Brilliant. / Just what I needed. / How very thoughtful of you. (all of these can mean the opposite).

Questioning a phrasing: That's one way of putting it. / I'm not sure that's the compliment you think it is. / Is that a joke, or are you serious?

Showing you caught the double meaning: I see what you did there. / Say no more. / Nudge, nudge. / Ah, now I get it.

Sharing a complaint or experience: Tell me about it. / You don't say. / No kidding. (the last two can be sincere or sarcastic).

Softening a criticism: It's not quite what I had in mind. / With respect, that may not be the best approach. / It could be a little more polished. (implied: it needs major changes).

Rejecting sarcastically: As if! / Yeah, right. / Like that's going to happen.

practice.title: Understatement
practice.instructions: Choose, complete or correct. Pay attention to the implied meaning.

items.prompt: After being lost for two days without water, a hiker says: 'It was a bit of an inconvenience.' The speaker is…
options: using understatement: the experience was terrible
items.explain: Implied: it was very serious; understatement lowers the volume of the words so the listener infers the gravity.

items.prompt: A: 'How was the concert?' B: 'Well, it wasn't ___ bad.' (= it was quite good)
answers: half
too
so
items.explain: Not half bad = quite good (implied: better than he expected).

items.prompt: In British English, 'That's quite good' most often implies…
options: it is acceptable but not impressive
items.explain: Quite softens: implied, it is somewhat below expectations.

items.prompt: A manager says: 'That's an interesting idea.' She probably means…
options: she has reservations and will probably not adopt it
items.explain: Implied: polite disagreement; "interesting" avoids direct rejection.

items.prompt: After a flood destroyed her ground floor, she called it 'a minor ___'.
items.explain: A mild word for a serious problem is understatement; the implied meaning is the real gravity.

items.prompt: I'm afraid there's a bit problem with your order.
answers: I'm afraid there's a bit of a problem with your order.
I am afraid there's a bit of a problem with your order.
I am afraid there is a bit of a problem with your order.
items.explain: A bit of a + noun; implied: the order has a real fault.

items.prompt: The launch lost half its budget in a week. 'That's not ___ what I'd call a success.'
answers: exactly
quite
precisely
items.explain: Not exactly = litotes; implied: it was a failure.

items.prompt: Put the words in order to form the sentence.
answers: I wouldn't say no to a second helping.
items.explain: I wouldn't say no to = litotes; implied: I accept gladly.

items.prompt: At a bus stop in pouring rain, someone says, 'Lovely weather!' What is meant?
options: The speaker wants to go to the beach
items.explain: Irony: the mismatch between the sentence and the situation signals the opposite.

items.prompt: Thank you a lot for ruining my day.
answers: Thanks a lot for ruining my day.
Thanks very much for ruining my day.
Thanks so much for ruining my day.
items.explain: "Thanks a lot" is the sarcastic thanks formula; implied: I am not grateful.

items.prompt: A: 'Are you coming to the party?' B: 'I have an exam at 8 tomorrow.' B implies…
options: B is not coming, or cannot stay long
B wants to discuss the exam
items.explain: Relevance implicature: the answer gives a reason for declining.

items.prompt: 'Some of the students passed.' What does the speaker typically imply?
items.explain: Scalar implicature: if all had passed, "all" would have been said.

items.prompt: 'Can you pass the salt?' is not really a question about your ___; it is a polite request.
answers: ability
items.explain: It is an indirect request; the implied meaning is "pass me the salt".

items.prompt: After a 12-hour day, a colleague mutters, 'Oh, great. Another meeting.' She is…
options: being sarcastic: she is dreading it
items.explain: "Oh, great" with a flat tone and a negative context = sarcasm.

items.prompt: He told me sarcastic that I was very clever.
answers: He told me sarcastically that I was very clever.
items.explain: An adverb is needed; implied: I thought the opposite.

items.prompt: Put the words in order to form the sentence.
answers: That's one way of putting it.
items.explain: "That's one way of putting it": implied, I would put it another way (blunter or more precise).

items.prompt: He talks as if he ___ the owner of the company, but he's only an intern.
answers: were
was
items.explain: Unreal in the present: were/was; implied: he isn't.

items.prompt: She looked at me as if I ___ two heads.
items.explain: Contrary-to-fact comparison: past simple; implied: she looked at me in puzzlement.

items.prompt: It looks as if it would rain any minute, so take an umbrella.
answers: It looks as if it's going to rain any minute, so take an umbrella.
It looks as if it is going to rain any minute, so take an umbrella.
It looks as if it will rain any minute, so take an umbrella.
items.explain: Real possibility: indicative, not "would".

items.prompt: He spent money as though there ___ no tomorrow.
answers: were
was
items.explain: As though + unreal past.

items.prompt: She reacted as if I ___ her a terrible insult. (I had only asked the time.)
items.explain: Earlier unreal event: past perfect; implied: she overreacted.

items.prompt: It's not ___ I care what he thinks.
answers: as if
as though
items.explain: It's not as if… = it's not that…; implied: I do care a little, or it bothers me that he thinks that way.

items.prompt: A: 'He says he'll finish by tomorrow.' B: 'As if!' B means…
options: I don't believe that for a moment
items.explain: As if! = sarcastic rejection.

items.prompt: Put the words in order to form the sentence.
answers: He behaved as though nothing had happened.
items.explain: As though + past perfect for something unreal; implied: she pretended nothing had happened.

practice.title: Puns and devices
practice.instructions: Identify the device and its meaning.

items.prompt: 'I used to be a banker, but I lost interest.' The pun plays on…
options: 'interest' as bank return and as curiosity
items.explain: Double meaning: stopped being interested / lost the bank interest.

items.prompt: 'She lost her keys and her temper.' This is an example of…
items.explain: A single verb (lost) with two complements of different meaning.

items.prompt: 'Deafening silence' is…
items.explain: Two contradictory terms: the implied meaning is a silence so intense it is almost loud.

items.prompt: A fire station burns to the ground. This is…
items.explain: An outcome contrary to expectation = situational irony.

items.prompt: The ___ is the final line of a joke, where the surprise or twist arrives.
answers: punchline
items.explain: Punchline = the final line of a joke.

items.prompt: He is a very sensible person; he cried when he heard the joke about his dog.
answers: He is a very sensitive person; he cried when he heard the joke about his dog.
He's a very sensitive person; he cried when he heard the joke about his dog.
items.explain: False friend: sensible = sensato; sensitive = sensible.

items.prompt: Put the words in order to form the sentence.
answers: It's the kind of humour that goes over my head.
items.explain: Go over someone's head = not to understand it; implied: the joke required knowledge I do not have.

items.prompt: A comedian tells a joke with a perfectly straight face, never smiling. This style is…
items.explain: Deadpan: the humour depends on the audience catching the joke without clues.

items.prompt: He said it with a perfectly straight face and no change of tone, so nobody knew he was joking. His humour was…
items.explain: Deadpan = without giving away the joke.

items.prompt: The newspaper ran a ___ of the president, exaggerating his habits for comic effect.
answers: parody
satire
lampoon
caricature
items.explain: Parody/satire: exaggeration for mocking or critical purposes.

items.prompt: 'Nice hat. Did you lose a bet?' is a…
items.explain: Wisecrack: a mocking remark; implied: the hat is ridiculous.

items.prompt: A comment said half-seriously, not meant to be taken literally, is…
items.explain: Tongue-in-cheek = said as a joke.

items.prompt: Trading ___ with colleagues over lunch makes the workday bearable.
answers: banter
items.explain: Banter = friendly teasing.

items.prompt: He is too ___ about serious matters; he treats funerals like open-mic nights.
items.explain: Flippant = frivolous; implied: a lack of respect.

items.prompt: She told a quip very witty.
answers: She told a very witty quip.
She made a very witty quip.
items.explain: The adjective precedes the noun.

items.prompt: The film is a biting ___ of corporate culture, exposing its absurdities through ridicule.
answers: satire
items.explain: Satire = criticism through mockery.

items.prompt: Stop ___ my leg! You didn't really meet the president.
answers: pulling
items.explain: Pull someone's leg = to tease someone; implied: I don't believe you.

items.prompt: They're just ___ you: the train hasn't been cancelled.
items.explain: Wind someone up = to annoy someone with a joke or trick.

items.prompt: She tried to ___ off the criticism with a smile.
answers: laugh
items.explain: Laugh something off = to dismiss its importance; implied: it hurt her.

items.prompt: His joke ___ completely; nobody laughed.
items.explain: Fall flat = to fail to work.

items.prompt: The comedian made fun with the politicians.
answers: The comedian made fun of the politicians.
The comedian poked fun at the politicians.
items.explain: Make fun of / poke fun at.

items.prompt: He told a story to ___ the ice at the awkward dinner.
items.explain: Break the ice = to ease tension.

items.prompt: I didn't ___ the joke until my sister explained it.
answers: get
understand
see
catch
items.explain: Get the joke = to understand the joke; implied: I missed the second reading.

items.prompt: 'He laughed it off' implies that he…
options: dismissed it lightly, perhaps to hide that it bothered him
items.explain: Laugh off = to play down, sometimes to hide discomfort.

items.prompt: Put the words in order to form the sentence.
answers: He talks as though he owned the place.
items.explain: As though + unreal past; implied: he behaves with an authority he does not have.

items.prompt: Put the words in order to form the sentence.
answers: Her wry smile suggested she knew more than she said.
items.explain: Wry smile: an ironic smile; implied: she knows something she is not saying.

items.prompt: Put the words in order to form the sentence.
answers: It's not as if anyone asked for his opinion.
items.explain: It's not as if…; implied: his opinion was not needed.

items.prompt: Put the words in order to form the sentence.
answers: The comedian poked fun at the whole cabinet.
items.explain: Poke fun at = to mock lightly.

items.prompt: Put the words in order to form the sentence.
answers: Nobody could tell whether he was serious or tongue-in-cheek.
items.explain: Tongue-in-cheek: said as a joke; irony without signalling it.

items.prompt: Put the words in order to form the sentence.
answers: She laughed off the criticism as if it were nothing.
items.explain: Laugh off + unreal "as if"; implied: it did matter to him.

write.prompt: Write a reflective essay (300 to 400 words) comparing how irony and humour are used in your culture with British understatement. Include at least three example sentences with their literal and implied meanings, a brief anecdote about a misunderstanding caused by missing irony, and several constructions with as if / as though. Opening example: In Mexico, as in Britain, saying exactly what one means is not always the goal of conversation…
targets: as if / as though + unreal past
checklist: Between 300 and 400 words
Three examples with literal and implied meaning explained
At least 3 correct uses of as if / as though (unreal past)
One understatement or litotes of your own, well formed (a bit of a…, not exactly…)
At least 5 words from the unit's humour vocabulary
An anecdote with a pragmatic misunderstanding
One sentence with a phrasal expression such as laugh off, wind up or fall flat
A conclusion with a personal stance
write.model:
In Mexico, as in Britain, saying exactly what one means is not always the goal of conversation. The difference lies in the direction the indirectness takes. Mexican humour tends towards exaggeration, wordplay and affectionate teasing; British humour favours understatement, the deadpan delivery and the wry aside. Both rely on the listener to read between the lines.

Take three British sentences. "That's not bad" literally denies a fault, but usually implies "that is excellent". "I was slightly disappointed" literally reports mild regret, yet it implies "I was furious". "With respect" literally promises courtesy and implies "I think you are wrong". My own contribution to the genre would be "It was not exactly my finest hour", which literally refers to a single poor hour and implies a complete catastrophe. Such litotes is a bit of a national sport.

I learned its dangers the hard way. Early in my career, a British colleague glanced at my first draft and said, "It's quite good." I thanked him warmly and submitted it, behaving as though he had said "excellent". When the document came back covered in corrections, I stared at it as if it had been written by somebody else. In his usage, "quite good" meant "acceptable, but needs work"; I had heard praise because, in Spanish, my instinct was to hear it that way. I could have laughed it off, but I wound up rewriting the whole report over a weekend.

Looking back, the episode amused me more than it stung. Irony is a kind of club, and its rules are rarely written down. A joke told tongue-in-cheek can fall flat if the audience is not in on it, and the banter that bonds one group can baffle another. It sometimes seems as if every culture speaks two languages: the one in the dictionary and the one hidden behind it. Even now, a quip delivered in perfect deadpan occasionally leaves me wondering whether I have been complimented or insulted.

Still, I would not trade the experience. Understanding irony in another language is the surest sign of having truly arrived in it, and I am proud to say that I now speak both dialects, though I confess I prefer to exaggerate.

checklist: Between 300 and 400 words

write.model:
"Well, that went rather well," said Clara, surveying the wreckage of the dinner. The soufflé lay in a sad heap on the floor, a candle had set fire to a napkin, and the guest of honour was picking trifle out of his hair.

Tom, who was extinguishing the napkin in the sink, did not look round. "Spectacular," he said. "I particularly admired the way the cat made an entrance."

Clara's smile did not reach her eyes. It was the smile of a woman who had stopped joking some time ago, though anyone who did not know her might have missed it.

Mr Hargreaves, however, did not know her. He beamed at her as though she had paid him a compliment. "I'm delighted you think so," he said. "I must say, I've rarely been to a dinner with such... energy."

"Energy," repeated Clara, deadpan.

"Quite. And the soufflé was a triumph. Might I have the recipe?"

There was a pause in which Tom, still facing the sink, seemed to struggle with a cough that was suspiciously like laughter. Clara looked at Mr Hargreaves as if he had asked her to lend him her car. He had, she realised, taken every word at face value, and was now gazing at her with the touching trust of a man who believed he had been given the best evening of his life.

"It's quite simple," she said, her voice wry. "You take six eggs, a great deal of optimism, and you drop the lot."

"Ha! Marvellous." Mr Hargreaves slapped his knee. "You're a wit, Clara."

"Well," quipped Tom, finally turning round, "we've certainly given him food for thought."

Clara threw a tea towel at him. It missed, as everything had that evening, and landed in the trifle.

"Rather well, indeed," she murmured, and, for the first time since seven o'clock, she laughed, properly and helplessly, as if the whole catastrophe had been rehearsed for the purpose. Mr Hargreaves, delighted, laughed too, and never learned why.

reading.title: Saying Less, Meaning More
reading.intro: Read the article and answer the questions. Pay attention to what is meant, not only to what is said.
paragraphs: Every culture has its rules for what may be said directly and what must be left to implication, but few elevate the art of leaving things unsaid quite as devotedly as the British. A visitor who is told that a proposal is 'interesting', that a dish is 'not unpleasant', or that a colleague's behaviour is 'a little unfortunate' would be wise to pause before celebrating. In a great many cases, the words on the surface and the message beneath them point in opposite directions.

Linguists would call this implicature: the gap between what is literally said and what a speaker intends the listener to infer. The philosopher Paul Grice argued that conversation runs on an unspoken agreement that speakers will be informative, truthful, relevant and clear. When someone appears to flout one of those expectations, listeners do not conclude that communication has failed; they search for a hidden meaning that would make the remark cooperative after all. If you ask a friend how her dreadful holiday went and she replies, 'Well, the hotel did have a roof,' she has told you almost nothing about the roof and almost everything about the hotel.

Understatement is the most familiar vehicle for this kind of indirection. A pilot announcing that passengers may experience 'a little turbulence' as the plane plunges, or a mountaineer describing a night spent in a blizzard as 'a bit chilly', is lowering the volume of his words precisely so that the listener will register how loud the reality was. The effect is partly comic, partly a display of composure: to refuse to dramatise a disaster is to signal that one is equal to it. This explains why understatement flourishes in cultures that prize emotional restraint, and why it can baffle visitors from those that do not, who may take 'it could have gone better' at face value when it was meant as a verdict on a catastrophe.

Irony works in the opposite direction, saying one thing while meaning its reverse, and sarcasm is irony sharpened into a weapon. Standing in a downpour and remarking 'lovely weather' is irony; telling a colleague who has just spilled coffee over your keyboard 'thanks, that's really helpful' is sarcasm, because it carries a target and a sting. Neither is signalled by grammar. Listeners rely on cues: an exaggerated stress, a deliberately flat tone, a pause, or simply the obvious mismatch between the remark and the situation. A comedian who delivers an outrageous line without a flicker of expression, the so-called deadpan style, forces the audience to do the interpretive work, and the pleasure of the joke lies partly in having done it.

Foreign learners often find that the hardest part is not recognising irony but producing it safely. A remark that would draw an appreciative smile among close friends may land as plain rudeness with a stranger, and the same words delivered in writing, without the benefit of tone, are notoriously prone to misreading. Many office disputes have begun with an email that was meant playfully and read as hostile. A practical rule is to reserve sarcasm for people whose reactions you can predict, and to tone down your irony in writing unless the relationship is secure.

There is also a subtler danger in taking understatement too literally on the receiving end. In one piece of workplace folklore, a manager responds to a draft report with the words, 'This is quite good, though perhaps you could consider a few small changes.' The author hears praise and goes home content. What the manager meant, as colleagues familiar with the idiom would have recognised at once, was that the report needed substantial rewriting. 'Quite' in this setting dilutes rather than intensifies; 'a few small changes' is a polite fiction; and 'perhaps you could consider' is not a suggestion but an instruction wrapped in good manners.

None of this means that British speakers are being dishonest. The convention is shared, and those within it decode the signals as automatically as they read a smile. The cost of indirectness is paid mostly by outsiders, who must learn the code; the benefit is that criticism can be delivered without open confrontation, and affection without sentimentality. A friend who says, 'You're not completely hopeless,' after watching you cook may well be offering the warmest compliment she can bring herself to utter. To understand such a remark is to have crossed a threshold: you are no longer merely hearing the language but listening to the people who speak it.

glossary.def: To openly disregard or break a rule or expectation.
To puzzle or confuse someone completely.
Calmness and self-control, especially under pressure.

A sharp, cutting quality, as in a remark that hurts or provokes.
A brief, faint sign or trace of something, such as an emotion.
To weaken or soften something by adding something else or reducing its force.
A low sound of complaint or annoyance; a grumble of displeasure.
To accept something as it appears, without questioning its hidden meaning.

listening.title: The meeting that went rather well
listening.intro: Listen to the conversation between three colleagues. You can repeat it.

lines.text: So, how did the meeting with Mr Whitlock go?
Oh, it went rather well. Apart from the part where he cancelled my project.
Ah. So 'rather well' is doing a lot of work in that sentence.
It's holding the whole thing up, frankly. He said my proposal was 'interesting' and that he'd 'give it some thought'.
Oh no. Dan, I've been there. 'I'll give it some thought' means no.
I'm beginning to realise that. He also said I'd 'clearly put a lot of effort in'.
Which is what you say about a school play when the lead has forgotten all his lines.
Don't be so unkind. Maybe he meant it kindly. He did say the slides looked 'nice'.
Priya, he said it the way you'd say it about a hospital waiting room.
Honestly, it's not as if you didn't warn us. You told us on Monday it might be 'a bit of a struggle'.
I did. I'd had a feeling. I just didn't expect the struggle to end in a funeral.
Right. Dramatic. Fancy a coffee? I'll buy. Consider it a condolence.
I wouldn't say no. Make mine a double.
Make it two. And Dan, rewrite the proposal. Mr Whitlock never says no; he just says 'interesting'.

items.prompt: What does Dan really mean by 'it went rather well'?

items.explain: Implied: it is a consolation compliment when the result was bad.

items.explain: Implied: "nice" is an empty compliment, without enthusiasm, for something that does not deserve it.

items.prompt: When Priya says, 'Consider it a condolence,' she is…

items.explain: Light humor: follows Dan's metaphor (funeral) to console him with a joke.

items.prompt: What is Marco's final advice?
options: Rewrite the proposal, because 'interesting' means rejection
items.explain: Implied: Whitlock never says no outright; "interesting" is their way of refusing.

tasks.prompt: Explain to a Spanish-speaking friend what these phrases really mean in a British context.

tasks.model: When a British colleague says 'That's an interesting idea', they often have reservations: it's a polite way of not committing. 'It could have gone better' is classic understatement, and it usually means the thing was a disaster. 'Not bad at all', on the other hand, is genuine praise: the speaker is using litotes to express a strong, but restrained, approval.

tasks.model: A colleague of mine once told a visiting manager, 'Well, that was a bit of an adventure,' after our train broke down for four hours. The manager looked at him as if he had enjoyed the whole thing and started asking where he'd found the adventure! My colleague had to explain, with a wry smile, that he meant it was a nightmare. We all laughed it off, but it taught me how easily understatement can be misunderstood.

tasks.prompt: Debate: are humour and irony universal, or do they depend on culture? Is sarcasm appropriate at work?

tasks.model: I'd say humour is only partly universal. Slapstick travels well, but irony and wordplay depend on shared knowledge, so they rarely survive translation. As for sarcasm at work, I'd tread carefully: it can lighten the mood among people who know each other well, but with a stranger it may land as plain rudeness. In my own experience, I've sometimes laughed along at a joke in English without really getting it, as if I had understood perfectly.

Contrast between universal and cultural humour
A warning about sarcasm, with examples
Humour vocabulary and as if / as though
